memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: When the whole nation had finished crossing the Jordan, the Lord said to Joshua, "Choose twelve men from among the people, one from each tribe, and tell them to take up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, from right where the priests are standing, and carry them over with you and put them down at the place where you stay tonight." — Josh 4:1-3 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The miracle was complete. The whole nation had crossed the flooded Jordan on dry ground. You might think God's next instruction would be about attacking Jericho or advancing quickly. Instead, God says, "Stop and gather some stones." Before pressing on to the next battle, God wanted them to build a memorial to what He had just done.

This tells us something about the heart of God. He knows how quickly we forget. Today's miracle can become tomorrow's faded memory. So God builds in a way for His people to remember. He does not want us rushing from blessing to blessing without ever pausing to mark His faithfulness.

Notice that the stones came "from the middle of the Jordan" — from the very place where God had held back the waters. The memorial was made of the miracle itself. Our reminders of God's goodness are best drawn from the actual places He has met us.

We are just as prone to forget. That is partly why the Lord Jesus gave us the bread and the cup, saying, "do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19). God graciously provides ways to help us remember His saving work, so that our gratitude stays fresh and our faith stays strong.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you pause to mark God's faithfulness, or rush from one thing to the next?
2. What "stones" could you gather to remember a time God came through for you?
3. How does remembering God's past faithfulness strengthen your faith today?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, I so easily forget what You have done. Help me pause and remember Your faithfulness, and keep my gratitude fresh. Amen.
